title: Paint the Grid So Neighbours Differ

concept.title: Colour cell by cell and look only at the two neighbours already painted
body: A grid with `r` rows and `c` columns must be painted with `k` colours so that two cells that **share an edge** have different colours. Paint the cells in reading order (row by row, left to right). When a cell is painted, only two of its neighbours are painted already: the one on the **left** and the one **above**. The other two will check against this cell later.

Again no undo is needed: the value `cells[pos]` is overwritten by the next try, and later cells only read cells with smaller positions. This "decide in an order in which every rule looks backwards" pattern is the simplest kind of backtracking. A single row of 10 cells with 4 colours already has `4 * 3^9 = 78732` colourings.

statement: A grid has `r` rows and `c` columns. Count the ways to paint every cell with one of `k` colours so that any two cells that share an edge (left-right or up-down) have different colours. The colours are different from each other.

examples.note: The top-left cell has 3 colours, the others follow: the 2 by 2 grid has 18 valid paintings with 3 colours.

hints: Paint the cells in reading order.
A cell has to differ from the cell on its left and the cell above it, when they exist.
The result of the loop does not need an undo step, because later cells only look at earlier cells.

explanation: The cells are painted in reading order; a colour is rejected when it equals the colour of the left or the upper neighbour. A fully painted grid counts one.
solution.complexity: Time proportional to the answer, up to about 80 000 paintings here; space O(r * c).
